entities.name: Richard FitzAlan, 8th Earl of Arundel
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard FitzAlan, 8th Earl of Arundel (c. 1267 – 17 March 1302), was a prominent English magnate whose life unfolded during the late 13th century, a pivotal era marked by King Edward I's ambitious consolidation of royal power and expansionist campaigns. As the hereditary holder of one of England's most ancient earldoms, FitzAlan's active military service positioned him at the heart of the Crown's relentless efforts to subjugate Wales and assert dominion over Scotland. His relatively brief but impactful career exemplifies the evolving dual role of the English peerage as both formidable feudal lords and essential military commanders in national conflicts.

Succeeding his father, John FitzAlan, 7th Earl of Arundel, in 1272, Richard became a royal ward until 1287. Upon reaching his majority, he immediately engaged in royal military ventures, notably serving in the Welsh Wars after the Statute of Rhuddlan. He played a crucial role in suppressing the significant rebellion led by Rhys ap Maredudd between 1287 and 1288, helping to cement English control over the newly conquered territories. Later, FitzAlan was a key figure in the nascent Scottish Wars, receiving summons for service against King John Balliol and Andrew Moray from 1297 onwards, and participating in the campaign that culminated in the Battle of Falkirk in 1298, where Edward I decisively defeated William Wallace's forces.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard FitzAlan's military service under Edward I significantly contributed to the English Crown's consolidation of power in Wales and its early campaigns in Scotland, representing the crucial role of the English peerage in royal expansionist policies. His career exemplifies the feudal obligations and military demands placed upon the English nobility during a period of intense royal centralization.
